turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, give me a second, this screen's decided to have a think. You're in about the chest, yes?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. It's nothing, honestly. Bit wheezy after a cold, that's all.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have you been wheezy?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Since the— actually, does this appointment count as a sick note? Work's being funny about it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): We can talk about a note at the end if you still want one. The wheeze, though. When did it start?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, after the cold — a week, two weeks, could be longer. I wasn't writing it down.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The office is boiling, everyone's got the same lurgy, it's doing the rounds.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I missed that — I was clicking the wrong tab. Fever. Have you actually felt feverish?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I stuck a thermometer under my tongue the other night and it was normal. No shivers.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit of a dry one. Worse at night. Doesn't stop me sleeping, so it's fine.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the wheeze — constant, or only when you're doing something?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Only if I leg it for the bus. Sometimes when I lie down. Hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): My blue inhaler's run out, that's the real reason I'm here. Chemist wouldn't just hand me another.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Prescription in a minute. Chest pain — yes or no?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Coughing any blood up? Or phlegm?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No blood. Tiny bit of clear stuff in the mornings. Nothing.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): You've got asthma on here since childhood, and you're twenty. Still the case?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Twenty last month. Mild asthma. I don't really do the asthma thing.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): What inhalers are you on? The screen's only half loaded.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Blue and brown. I get them mixed up, always have.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): When you're wheezy, which one do you actually use?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Whichever I grab. The brown one sometimes, 'cause it's... no, the blue works faster. I think blue's the emergency one. Or is brown?
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blue is salbutamol, the reliever. Brown is the steroid preventer. Do you know the name on the brown canister?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No idea. Clen-something. I binned the box months ago.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? This machine just pinged and I lost the last bit.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I said I binned the box. I don't know the name.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, it's come up. Clenil, beclometasone, two hundred micrograms, two puffs twice a day. That the brown one?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Suppose so. I don't take it twice a day. Only when the wheeze is actually annoying, which is rare.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the blue one, salbutamol — how often?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Hardly. Once, if that.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Once in a day?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, not today. Today's been a bit more. I don't count them.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I do need a rough number.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Maybe five, six times a day. Two puffs. Only while this cold's hanging about. Normally I'm absolutely fine.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five or six is a lot, even if you're playing it down.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not a lot. It's just a cold.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies? Anything on that, penicillin or otherwise?

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't think so. My mum told some doctor I got a rash with penicillin when I was little, so it's probably written down, but I've never noticed anything. I'm not even sure it happened.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): So penicillin's a maybe. No definite reaction you remember.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Exactly. Can we skip it.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoking?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really smoking. A few at the weekend if I'm out. Doesn't affect anything.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry — weekend, did you say? The cursor's jumped.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Weekends. A few cigarettes. Can we move on.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nurse has put your peak flow in. First blow 310, second 340. Best we've got on the record for you is 560.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't do it properly, I was mid-sentence. Those things never work on me.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): She's also written sats 96 percent, pulse 98, breathing rate 18. No temperature on the chart.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): So basically normal. I knew it.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen. Big breath in, and out.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to cough? I'd rather not.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Just the breath, that's it. You've got a wheeze both sides, louder breathing out. No crackles. Throat looks a bit red.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Red throat, there you go, it's the cold.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone ever done formal breathing tests, the spirometry?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Last year at the hospital. They said it was borderline. No number, just borderline, and to come back if I got worse. I didn't bother.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Borderline, and you didn't get the figures. Alright.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): It was ages ago anyway. Irrelevant.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was going to skip tablets, just tell you to use the brown inhaler properly and see you next week.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine by me. I don't want tablets.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on. Five or six times a day on the reliever, and peak flow down at 340 from 560 — I'm changing that. You do need a steroid course.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Prednisolone? My cousin went on that and she—
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, you trailed off. She what?
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Doesn't matter. She put on weight. I'm not being funny but I'm not doing months of that.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not months. I did briefly think of a chest x-ray too, but no, I won't send you for one. This is an asthma flare after the virus.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. So what am I actually taking?
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): Prednisolone forty milligrams, once each morning, with food, for five days, then stop. I nearly put thirty, but forty is the one I want.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I feel fine on day two I can bin them, yeah?

[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. Finish the five days. Brown inhaler, the beclometasone, two puffs twice a day every single day, even when you feel fine. Blue one, two puffs when you need it, not on a schedule.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): The blue canister's empty though. And I think it might say 200 on it, not 100. I never look properly.

[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): The record says salbutamol 100 micrograms. I'll issue a replacement on that. If you get home and the old canister clearly says 200, ring the surgery and tell us, because that doesn't match.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I'll try and remember. No promises.
[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in three days, we'll repeat the peak flow. If you can't finish a sentence, or your lips go blue, don't wait — A&E, not the walk-in.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days for a sniffle is mad, but alright. Are we done? I've got a train.

No temperature was recorded on the chart.
Previous spirometry was last year at the hospital, reported to the patient as 'borderline', with advice to come back if worse; no figures were given and the patient did not return.
Doctor initially considered managing without tablets and reviewing next week, then changed plan because of reliever use and reduced peak flow.
Doctor briefly considered a chest X-ray but decided not to send for one.
Prednisolone was specifically advised to be taken with food.

omissions.text: Patient reports the salbutamol inhaler is currently empty/run out, not just that they use it 5–6 times/day.

Beclometasone/Clenil adherence is poor: patient says they do not take it twice daily and only use it when the wheeze is annoying, which is rare. Recording it simply as currently used 2 puffs twice a day is misleading.

Salbutamol use frequency is uncertain overall: patient initially says 'hardly' and then, during this illness, estimates maybe 5–6 times a day, 2 puffs each time; they also say not today initially but then correct that today has been more. This downplaying/uncertainty is not captured.
